findings.headline: Draft 3 opens with a death threat that immediately raises stakes; Draft 2 opened with surveillance logistics
findings.priorDraft: Draft 2's opening phone exchange between Cypher and Trinity is a procedural report: Cypher lists Neo's 7-11 purchase and commute route. The inciting danger is implied but buried under mundane detail. The audience has no reason to feel urgency before Trinity is cornered in room 303.
findings.currentDraft: Draft 3 opens with Cypher saying 'We're going to kill him. Do you understand that? He's going to die just like the others.' This is the first line spoken in the film. The mortal stakes for Neo are declared before we see a single image of the world. The inciting threat arrives in the first seconds of page 1, well inside the p.10 requirement.

evidence.excerpt:
CYPHER (V.O.)
We're going to kill him. Do you understand that? He's going to die just like the others.
TRINITY (V.O.)
Morpheus believes he is the One.
CYPHER (V.O.)
Do you?

findings.headline: Trinity's revised non-answer in scene 1 replaces expository hedging with a loaded silence
findings.priorDraft: In Draft 2, Trinity's response to Cypher's doubt is 'I think Morpheus knows things that I don't,' a deflection that still functions as information delivery: it tells the audience Morpheus is the authority. The exchange runs five more beats explaining the surveillance situation.
findings.currentDraft: Draft 3 compresses Trinity's response to 'I... it doesn't matter what I believe.' The hesitation before the contraction, written into the line itself, does more emotional work than the prior draft's full paragraph. Her belief is the subject the scene is about, and she refuses to answer directly. That refusal is the subtext.

evidence.excerpt:
CYPHER (V.O.)
Do you?
TRINITY (V.O.)
I... it doesn't matter what I believe.

findings.headline: The Baudrillard beat in scene 12 shows Neo's want as embodied action rather than a passive computer prompt
findings.priorDraft: In Draft 2, the white rabbit sequence reaches Neo through an anonymous screen message. Neo's engagement with the mystery is reactive: he reads, he answers the door, he agrees to go. His want is stated by the screen ('Do you want to know what the Matrix is') rather than demonstrated by him.
findings.currentDraft: Draft 3 adds the specific physical detail that Neo hides the disc inside a copy of Baudrillard's 'Simulacra and Simulations.' This is a single action that shows Neo actively living the question about the nature of reality before anyone asks it of him. His want is now demonstrated through behavior, not prompted by an on-screen instruction.

evidence.excerpt: CHOI buys a disc. Neo hides it inside Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulations.

findings.headline: The Construct explanation sequence at scene 39 remains a lecture block with no scene break or interruption
findings.priorDraft: In Draft 2, the hovercraft sequence in which Morpheus explains the year, the machines, the power plant, and the Oracle prophecy is presented as an unbroken block of expository dialogue attributed to a single scene heading: INT. HOVERCRAFT.
findings.currentDraft: Draft 3 consolidates the same information under INT. CONSTRUCT at scene 39, still as an uninterrupted Morpheus monologue. The coppertop battery is a new visual prop, which is a gain, but the structural problem is unchanged: one character explains the entire history of the world to another in a single scene with no dramatic pressure or interruption to force economy.

evidence.excerpt:
MORPHEUS
This is the world as it exists today. The desert of the real. The machines grow humans.
(holds up a coppertop battery)
What is the Matrix? Control.

findings.headline: The Oracle scene loses its explicit false-prophecy reversal, weakening the midpoint pivot
findings.priorDraft: Draft 2's Oracle scene at the Temple of Zion contains a clear, declarative reversal: 'You're not the One. Sorry, kid.' This is a textbook midpoint false defeat. Neo is told by the person whose judgment he sought that he is not what Morpheus believes him to be. The dramatic consequence is immediate and legible.
findings.currentDraft: Draft 3 replaces that direct statement with a cryptic analogy: 'Being the One is just like being in love. Nobody can tell you you're in love. You just know it.' The Oracle no longer says Neo is not the One. The reversal has become ambiguous. The midpoint now reads as a riddle rather than a setback, which diffuses the structural turn the second half depends on.

evidence.excerpt:
ORACLE
Know Thyself. Being the One is just like being in love. Nobody can tell you you're in love. You just know it. Through and through. Balls to bones.
ORACLE
You're going to have to make a choice.

findings.headline: Neo's final monologue is rewritten as a declaration of action rather than a self-description
findings.priorDraft: Draft 2's closing Neo monologue is retrospective and expository: 'I've decided to make a few changes.' Neo describes his own arc to the audience. The visual button, flying out of the phone booth, is undercut by dialogue that tells us what to think about it.
findings.currentDraft: Draft 3 replaces self-description with direct address to the system: 'I'm going to show these people what you don't want them to see.' The thematic payload is delivered as a threat aimed outward, not an announcement aimed at the audience. The line earns the image of flight rather than explaining it.

evidence.excerpt:
NEO (V.O.)
I know you're out there. I can feel you now. I know that you're afraid. I'm going to show these people what you don't want them to see. A world where anything is possible. To be free, you cannot change your cage. You have to change yourself.
(Neo hangs up and flies into the sky.)

summary.note: Draft 3 is a meaningful step forward on voice and opening mechanics, but steer the student toward the midpoint regression: the Oracle's ambiguity is thematically richer but structurally costly, and the workshop should pressure-test whether the second half still earns its momentum without a clean false-defeat beat. The Construct lecture block is the most fixable unaddressed problem and is a good entry point for a scene-economy conversation, since the coppertop battery already shows the student knows how to externalize information visually.
